verdicts.rewritten_summary: French prison-system reporting: the controller-general of detention places finds trans detainees — overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement — suffer the most in prison; administration policy recognises only biological sex (a 2011 Nantes case placed a trans woman in a men's prison). BLM detainees fall under this French system.

Dossier on BLM trans rights: the French framework applies — legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

Travel guide: 'full equality' under French law on ~8 square miles and ~10,000 residents; luxury-yacht economy long welcoming to gay couples with zero visible scene — discretion is the norm and same-sex couples attract no attention.

Aggregate rating 7.7/10 (9 positive rights, 1 red flag): legal gender change without surgery, anti-discrimination law in place but limited healthcare access; no government LGBT+ travel advice (FCDO shows no warnings); no trans-specific visitor tips yet submitted.

Luxury-operator guide: low crime, open and accepting culture with no Pride-specific events, staff trained for diverse guests; visitors are high-end and discreet — no LGBTQ venues or scene, but no hostility noted.

HRW (12 Apr 2024): Belarusian law redefines 'pornography' to include depictions of same-sex relationships and transgender people, classed with necrophilia/paedophilia as 'non-traditional relationships'; production punishable by up to 4 years (13 for child material). Explicitly aimed at LGBT dignity — a persecution vector for visitors and residents alike.

JURIST (28 Sep 2024): TG House Belarus reports 15+ LGBTQ people detained in one month, incl. 8 transgender — most charged with hooliganism, two with pornography; custody abuse (physical and psychological) reported and some fled the country.

UNPR review coverage (2018): Belize accepted 15 of 17 SOGI recommendations — the first CARICOM country to accept that many — pledging legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and SOGI data collection; two rights-equality recommendations 'noted' rather than accepted.

Belize Supreme Court, 10 Aug 2016 (Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin): colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law struck down as unconstitutional — the challenge LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco filed in 2010; landmark decriminalisation for the country.

Expat overview (2019): after the 2016 ruling — first former British Caribbean colony to overturn its anti-sodomy law — gay travellers have long found Belize friendly, though the rarely-enforced law had fostered intolerance (a 1998 gay-cruise docking protest shows residual hostility).

Live coverage (2013) of the constitutional challenge to Section 53: Unibam's Orozco case tested in Belize City, with day-by-day courtroom dispatches — the litigation that eventually produced the 2016 strike-down.

Governor's assent (Feb 2018) to the Domestic Partnerships Act: passed House and Senate, replacing same-sex marriage with a domestic partnership open to same-sex and heterosexual couples — rights include intestate inheritance, partner pensions, property, medical decision-making and residency as a Bermudian's partner. Among the first English-speaking CARICOM islands to legislate recognition.

Social climate: Bermuda's AME and other churches protested a gay cruise (Norwegian Dawn, New York–Bermuda, July 12) as 'incompatible with the word of God and the Christian moral fibre' — organised religious hostility to visible same-sex couples.

AP (4 Jul 2013): Human Rights Amendment Act passed the Senate unopposed after House debate — outlaws discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds, amending the 30-year-old Human Rights Act (signed by the governor).

Royal Gazette (14 May 1994): the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to decriminalise consensual sex between adult men, removing two Criminal Code sections — a debate that split the island, with religious leaders divided and the Christian Coalition staging marches against it.

Newsweek (Jul 2017): after the US trans military ban, only 18 countries are believed to fully legalise LGBT military service — international baseline for whether trans visitors/soldiers face service exclusion; Bolivia not singled out in the text.

Legal-profile page: Constitution prohibits discrimination and guarantees bodily integrity (Art 15(II) violence, 45(V) maternity), Penal Code Title VIII governs abortion. Superseded by post-2016 law: 2016 gender-identity law (self-ID), Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion, Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition for same-sex couples.
verdicts.note: superseded: Post-2017 developments the archived sources miss: Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion; Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition; 2016 gender-identity law remains a world-leading baseline. 2024 article still current.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: eju.tv/La Razón (25 Aug 2014, Spanish): homosexuality is taboo in Bolivia's armed forces — gay soldiers report discrimination and sanctions, testimony given anonymously; the TLGB collective and human-rights activists demand openness.
Overview: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013; legal gender change without surgery allowed since 2018 (STF); age of consent equal; plus federal anti-discrimination framework.

Country overview (updated Mar 2026): constitutional and federal criminal provisions — after the 2019 Supreme Court ruling — prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, yet LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination in practice.
Expat legal guide (updated 5 Apr 2026): same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules — the practical family/entry framework a trans visitor or partner needs.
Investigation (May 2024): 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies victimise LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo; the city prepares for a Pride drawing thousands of tourists.

São Paulo Court of Justice (27th Private Chamber) upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing — the Barra Bonita first instance had ordered R$4,000 compensation.

Analysis (2022): lower courts pushed the Superior Court of Justice (STJ) toward unanimously extending Maria da Penha Law and Feminicide Law remedies to trans women — inclusion of trans people in violence-prevention law.
Official page of the São Paulo Municipal Council's parliamentary inquiry (CPI) on Violence Against Trans and Travesti Persons — final report concluded carrying 189 recommendations.

Canada travel advisory (updated Aug 2026): 'Exercise a high degree of caution' — high crime rates and gang-related urban violence; avoid demonstrations and border drug-trafficking zones. Dated country-wide baseline for visitors.
Tour operator guide: Brazil 'progressive' on LGBTQIA+ rights and generally safe, but flags that practical safety issues can arise for LGBTQIA+ travellers.
Historical essay (Mar 2000): historian James N. Green on early-1900s Rio homosexual subculture — Glória monument site functioning as a meeting venue in the 'tropical Paris' era.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Erasing 76 Crimes (Nov 2018): second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil held in Barbados (with NOW, local ally, veteran trans advocates named); trans activist Alexa Hoffmann's first-person account of visibility and danger on the island.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Apr 2019): sentencing in the violent meat-cleaver attack on trans activist Alexa Hoffmann — no jail time handed down; reported via Maurice Tomlinson and the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network — an impunity outcome visitors should weigh.

Commentary (Aug 2020): trans Barbadians are frequently fired or denied jobs for 'dressing wrong'; the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill does not cover them, and the island's 'Welcome Stamp' remote-work visa markets openness while anti-gay law stands.

Xtra (Jun 2018): Barbadian activists filed a constitutional challenge to the anti-gay laws with Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: BBC (3 Apr 2019): stage 3 of the Syariah Penal Code took effect — stoning for anal sex and adultery, amputation for theft, 40 strokes of the cane for lesbian sex; homosexuality was already illegal with up to 10 years. The law mostly applies to Muslims (~two-thirds of the 420,000 population); Brunei has carried out no execution since 1957. Freshness check 2026-09-27: still in force, 2019 moratorium on executions intact.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: HRW '#OUTLAWED' global map: at least 67 countries criminalise same-sex relations and at least nine criminalise gender expression; Brunei is one of at least two (with Oman) whose national laws expressly criminalise 'posing as' or 'imitating' a person of a different sex — the record's trans-specific offence, alongside Malaysia's state-sharia analogue.

US State Dept 2017 report: the Syariah Penal Code bans men dressing as women or women dressing as men 'without reasonable excuse', with no known convictions in 2017; 'liwat' between men carries death by stoning if implemented, and the report records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services. Morality provisions (cross-dressing, alcohol, Ramadan eating, religious propagation) were enforced; sharia implementing regulations were still unissued.
